stories.title: HUMAIN and DataVolt sign framework agreement with Nebius for large-scale campus in Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: HUMAIN, an artificial intelligence company owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), and DataVolt, a Saudi Arabia-based large-scale data center infrastructure developer, owner and operator, have announced a preliminary framework agreement with Nebius, an AI cloud company, for data center capacity at Oxagon, NEOM’s advanced industrial city on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast. stories.content:
HUMAIN, an artificial intelligence company owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), and DataVolt, a Saudi Arabia-based large-scale data center infrastructure developer, owner and operator, have announced a preliminary framework agreement with Nebius, an AI cloud company, for data center capacity at Oxagon, NEOM’s advanced industrial city on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast.

Readers would recall that in August this year, HUMAIN and DataVolt had announced an expanded partnership to develop 100 MW of the 360 MW AI-ready data center at Oxagon. Under the proposed framework, Nebius would become an anchor customer for the planned AI giga campus, with the contemplated offtake representing up to 50 MW, which is half of the initial 100 MW currently under construction as part of the first phase’s planned 360 MW.

The Nebius agreement was signed on the sidelines of NVIDIA’s GTC Berlin conference. The proposed capacity allocation is expected to become operational in phases from Q4 2027.

“The real measure of AI infrastructure is not how much capacity you build, but the demand you can secure and the value you can deliver,” said Tareq Amin, CEO, HUMAIN. “Advancing our commercial relationship with Nebius as our first customer is a significant milestone for HUMAIN and a clear demonstration of the international demand for the infrastructure we are developing.”

“Speed to market and infrastructure cost competitiveness will define the winners in the global AI compute race,” said Rajit Nanda, CEO, DataVolt. “At Oxagon, we are building at scale, with a clear focus on delivering highly competitive infrastructure costs. By combining Saudi Arabia’s energy advantages with disciplined execution, we are helping create a platform for the Kingdom to compete globally in AI compute, not just as an energy powerhouse, but as an exporter of digital capacity.”

“The agreement between HUMAIN, DataVolt and Nebius reflects growing global demand for AI ready infrastructure and NEOM’s role in enabling advanced industries,” said Eng. Aiman Al-Mudaifer, MD & CEO, NEOM. “This partnership demonstrates how NEOM is translating its strategic priorities into tangible opportunities that deliver lasting economic impact.”

Oxagon aims to position itself as an advanced industrial ecosystem that offers the potential to combine low latency digital connectivity, developed land and scalable energy within a purpose-built environment, enabling it to support large-scale AI infrastructure serving customers across global markets. The campus is designed to support AI workloads, with Nebius expected to deploy NVIDIA-powered computing infrastructure under the agreement to meet growing demand for its AI cloud.

stories.title: Could market volatility delay DayOne’s IPO?
stories.summary: DayOne Data Centers (DayOne), a Singapore based data center operator, is reportedly considering delaying its planned US initial public offering (IPO) or reducing the size of the share sale amid growing volatility in the data center sector. The company was previously considering raising US$ 5 billion through the IPO, potentially in the fourth quarter, with […]
stories.content:
DayOne Data Centers (DayOne), a Singapore based data center operator, is reportedly considering delaying its planned US initial public offering (IPO) or reducing the size of the share sale amid growing volatility in the data center sector. The company was previously considering raising US$ 5 billion through the IPO, potentially in the fourth quarter, with a targeted valuation of approximately US$ 20 billion.

According to a report from Bloomberg, the company has been assessing market conditions while waiting for an opportune window to launch the listing. One option under consideration is to postpone the IPO until market sentiment improves.

Alternatively, DayOne could proceed with a smaller offering targeting between US$ 2.5 billion and US$ 3 billion, approximately half its original fundraising target. Backed by investors including Coatue and Hillhouse, DayOne continues to engage with prospective investors and remains keen to proceed with the listing as soon as market conditions permit, the people said.

DayOne had filed a Form F-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for its proposed IPO of ADSs on Nasdaq under the ticker “DODC” in early October. Morgan Stanley, J.P. Morgan, BofA Securities and Citigroup were appointed as underwriters, while the offering size and price range had yet to be determined.

So far, Day One itself has not made any official statement about any postponement. Discussions are still ongoing and DayOne could still proceed with the offering in the coming weeks, depending on market conditions. The latest considerations highlight the challenges facing data center operators seeking to tap public markets amid heightened volatility and shifting investor sentiment towards the sector.

stories.title: AI workloads challenge traditional UPS infrastructure in data centers
stories.summary: AI is reshaping data center power infrastructure, requiring new considerations for uninterruptible power supply (UPS) systems. Higher rack densities and dynamic loads necessitate advanced UPS capabilities.
stories.content:
AI workloads are fundamentally altering data center planning and design, impacting power infrastructure, rack density, and load profiles.Traditional UPS decisions focused on uptime, footprint, and efficiency remain important, but AI introduces new power challenges.These include higher rack densities, rapidly changing dynamic loads, faster deployment timelines, and growing grid constraints.UPS solutions must now support increasing AI density, respond to dynamic load behavior, scale with deployments, be deployed quickly, and adapt to evolving grid requirements.Some of the latest AI platforms require rack densities exceeding 100 kW, with some approaching 230 kW per rack.This significantly departs from the average 10-15 kW per rack environments common only a few years ago.AI workloads are also more dynamic than traditional data center loads, creating rapid power fluctuations within milliseconds.UPS technologies with power smoothing capabilities can help mitigate these fluctuations by intelligently charging and discharging battery systems.Modular UPS architectures offer scalability and faster deployment, reducing overprovisioning while providing flexibility for future growth.Furthermore, power infrastructure must increasingly support the broader electrical ecosystem due to growing AI workloads.Capabilities such as Fault Ride-Through (FRT) allow UPS systems to remain operational during short-duration voltage disturbances.Fast Frequency Reserve (FFR) provides another layer of grid support, responding rapidly to frequency fluctuations.This gives utilities time to stabilise the grid and helps prevent blackouts.

stories.title: Cardiff data centre considers gas power due to grid delays
stories.summary: Curtis Hall's proposed Cardiff data centre may use temporary gas-fired generation for up to five years. This is due to potential grid connection delays for its 150MW capacity until 2034.
stories.content:
Curtis Hall is considering building a temporary energy centre powered by gas for its proposed data centre in Cardiff, Wales. This move addresses significant grid connection delays, with the full 150MW capacity potentially unavailable until sometime between 2030 and 2034.The developer proposes a temporary energy centre with up to 49.9MW of gas-fired generation. This temporary plant could operate from July 2028 until approximately July 2033, using gas turbines continuously.The 49.9MW capacity is notable as it falls just below the 50MW threshold. This threshold triggers Wales’ Significant Infrastructure Projects consenting regime, which requires Welsh ministerial approval for larger generating stations.
### Broader UK Data Centre Power Challenges

The situation in Cardiff reflects a wider trend in the UK data centre sector, where grid delays are prompting developers to explore alternative power strategies. Another proposed 72MW data centre near Reading plans for 49.9MW of natural gas fuel cells for its initial development.This project faces similar challenges, with secured grid reinforcement for a 60MVA connection not expected until 2037. Such delays suggest that microgrids may become essential for future data centre growth in the UK. This will be the case until sufficient grid reinforcement is completed.

stories.title: Malaysia proposes bill to regulate data center industry
stories.summary: Malaysia has proposed a Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill to regulate its booming data center industry. This follows Singapore's recent Digital Infrastructure Act and addresses anticipated capacity constraints.
stories.content:
Malaysia has proposed the Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill to regulate its rapidly growing data center industry, a move that follows Singapore's recent Digital Infrastructure Act.The proposed legislation aims to tighten requirements for data center developers, focusing on capacity reservations and utility costs. The National Economic Action Council (NEAC), led by the prime minister, has already agreed to the bill, which is expected to be submitted to the Cabinet by 2027.The country is projected to become the largest data center hub in Asia, excluding China, by 2030. This growth necessitates new rules to ensure local benefits from substantial investments and resource consumption.As of July, the Data Centre Task Force has approved 27 projects with an estimated investment of RM225.97 billion. Of these, 16 are in Johor, 10 in Selangor, and one in Negeri Sembilan, with all but one currently under construction.A significant gap exists between reserved power capacity and actual demand. As of August, 45 operating facilities demanded approximately 1.37 GW, while the combined maximum load was 6 GW.Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani proposed that data center developers bear transmission upgrade costs. He also suggested operators pay for committed electricity capacity they do not use, aiming to reduce the discrepancy.Deputy Prime Minister Fadillah Yusof proposed a "user-pays" electricity pricing mechanism and higher Connected Load Charges. These measures are intended to discourage excessive power reservations. Fadillah also encouraged independent generation and disclosed 12.3 GW of approved electricity supply capacity against an 8.39 GW projected maximum demand by 2030.Data centers will also need to account for their water demand, with approved demand across Johor, Selangor, and Negeri Sembilan at 445.04 million litres daily over 2025–2030.The approved projects now include a minimum 30 per cent local content requirement, monitored via six-monthly reports. These 27 projects are expected to generate 4,053 jobs, with Malaysians projected to fill 89.21 per cent of the highly skilled positions.

stories.title: Climate Collective explores water-tech accelerator, data centre programme
stories.summary: Climate Collective Foundation is exploring a digital water-tech accelerator for municipalities and industry. This is alongside a planned 2027 programme to address data centres’ energy and water challenges.
stories.content:
Climate Collective Foundation (CCF) is exploring a digital water-tech accelerator to help municipalities and industrial users measure and reduce water consumption, Pratap Raju, founder of CCF, told Dataquest.The proposed initiative would connect water-tech startups with users and funding partners. CCF is also planning a technology-sourcing accelerator for 2027 in Visakhapatnam. This programme will identify and validate solutions for data centres’ energy, water, and biodiversity impacts.The plans follow discussions at Bangalore Climate Data Week 2026, which covered artificial intelligence (AI) for climate action. These discussions also addressed the resource requirements of AI infrastructure.
### Water Management and Impact Assessment

Measurement is a key problem in water management, Raju said. Without reliable consumption data, municipalities, industrial parks, and residential communities struggle to establish reduction plans.“Without measurement, it's hard to get the demand to create plans to reduce water usage in municipalities, in industrial parks, in residential areas,” Raju said. He noted some Indian digital water-tech startups have reached revenues of ₹20–40 crore. Raju did not identify the companies or specify the timeframe for their revenue growth.Climate Collective has developed a methodology to assess climate technologies’ environmental impact. This is done through its Climate Tech Impact Platform. The approach compares a technology’s “handprint”—environmental savings enabled by customer use—with its “footprint”—resources consumed in manufacturing and operating.“The handprint approach is basically, if I give you, the client, the solution, what are the savings in energy, water, or waste from you using the technology?” Raju said. He added that CCF developed the methodology over four years. Impact funds in India have adopted the platform.
### Data Centre Accelerator in Visakhapatnam

The Visakhapatnam accelerator aims to help data centre operators and other industrial users. It will help them find technologies that have demonstrated effectiveness in addressing electricity, water, and biodiversity challenges. Raju said sourcing teams at large organisations are often too small to evaluate global solutions.Electricity demand presents a particular challenge at the local level. Large facilities can add substantial loads to grids that take time to expand, Raju said. Demand response, where data centres adjust computing workloads during grid pressure, is an opportunity for startups.Water consumption and biodiversity impacts are also concerns. Raju said newer air-cooled and closed-loop cooling systems could reduce water use. This impact would depend on the technology and facility.AI-enabled climate solutions could reach the pilot stage faster and with less initial capital. Some AI-based solutions can reach a minimum viable product within three to six months. This compares to one to three years for many physical climate technologies, Raju said. A high-quality pilot with an industry or government customer could be feasible within 12 to 15 months.

stories.title: AI era magnifies data centre investment risks
stories.summary: Investment challenges in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure are intensifying, with familiar risks now appearing at a larger scale. Panellists at Capacity Europe noted that power constraints and permitting delays are key hurdles.
stories.content:
The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming infrastructure investment, magnifying traditional risks for data centres, according to panellists at Capacity Europe. Development hurdles include power constraints, permitting delays, technology requirements, and customer demand, they said.Dharman Sury of BGO Data Centers, Zach Gellman of DigitalBridge, Oliver Felice-Owens of Guggenheim, and Paul McNally of Echelon Data Centres participated in the panel, chaired by Venessa Moffat of the Data Centre Alliance.
### Evolving Risk Landscape

The panellists generally agreed that while the risks are not entirely new, their scale and complexity have increased. Mr McNally argued that traditional concerns around development, credit, and execution are now magnified by new levels of investment.Mr Gellman noted that AI infrastructure presents familiar risks in novel ways. Investors previously relied on stable assumptions about equipment lifecycles and upgrade needs. However, rapid changes in use cases now necessitate rethinking upgrade and maintenance capital expenditure assumptions.The investor base is also changing, with new entrants such as pension funds and sovereign wealth funds pursuing different risk-return strategies, Mr Gellman added.
### Social Licence Criticality

Mr Gellman emphasised the critical importance of a "social licence" for data centre investors. He cited Loudoun County, Virginia, where data centres contribute approximately half of local tax revenues, funding public services.This highlights the need for clear communication of benefits to local communities, especially as public scrutiny on AI infrastructure grows. Panellists concluded that predictability will be vital for confident capital deployment in this complex environment.

stories.summary: India's information technology (IT) services sector saw investments rise to 4.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) between Q42025 and Q32026. This increase, driven by new data centre projects, represents a significant jump from 0.8 per cent a year prior.
stories.content:
Investments in India’s information technology (IT) services sector reached 4.5 per cent of the gross domestic product (GDP) over the 12-month period from Q42025 through Q32026, according to a research note by Nomura. This marks an increase from 0.8 per cent during the same period a year earlier.New data centre projects and an upward revision in the cost of existing projects were key drivers for this rise, Nomura said. The IT sector’s share accounted for approximately 28.4 per cent of total new investment projects announced.A tax holiday for foreign companies, mentioned in Union Budget 2026-27, also buoyed these investment announcements, Nomura reported, citing data from the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE).Despite the encouraging rise in announcements, Nomura cautioned that the availability of power and water remains a key constraint for project execution.India is experiencing a structural shift, with rising services imports impacting its services trade surplus, Nomura noted. Increased imports of consultancy, digital, technical, and trade services could be attributed to the growing importance of Global Capability Centres (GCCs), artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, and a focus on data centres, alongside rising intellectual property (IP) imports.Nomura partly attributed the rising IP imports to lower domestic research and development spending. India’s current account deficit increased by $3.5 billion year-on-year in the April-August period of FY27, despite cushioning from remittances and a services surplus.

stories.title: Exelon eyes return to regulated power generation amid demand surge
stories.summary: Exelon, a regulated utility, is expanding its transmission business and advocating for a greater role in power generation. This shift is driven by surging data center demand and tightening grid capacity within the PJM Interconnection region.
stories.content:
Exelon, a transmission and distribution utility holding company, is expanding its transmission business and advocating for a larger role in power generation, according to Carim Khouzami, its executive vice president of transmission and development.This strategic re-evaluation comes four years after separating from Constellation Energy, driven by rising data center demand, tightening capacity reserves, and shortcomings in PJM’s wholesale markets.
### Expanding Transmission and Capital Investment

Exelon, which operates six utilities serving approximately 10.9 million electric and gas customers across seven jurisdictions, projects $41.7 billion in capital expenditures from 2026 through 2029. This marks an increase from its earlier $31.3 billion plan for 2023–2026.Transmission’s share of this spending has risen from 21 per cent to 39 per cent, representing $16.3 billion in the current plan. The company also identifies an additional $12 billion to $17 billion in potential transmission opportunities beyond its existing capital programme, including competitive projects outside its traditional service territories.The utility has already secured approval for $700 million in independently submitted projects and participated in another $1.7 billion in projects jointly developed with NextEra Energy Transmission within PJM’s 2025 Regional Transmission Expansion Plan. Exelon is also pursuing opportunities in the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s long-range transmission programme.
### Addressing Soaring Data Center Demand

Exelon identifies approximately 11 GW of high-probability large load across its service territories, including 9 GW in Commonwealth Edison (ComEd)’s northern Illinois territory and 2 GW in the Mid-Atlantic. Another 25 GW of potential demand is undergoing or awaiting study.Khouzami noted that ComEd’s high-probability demand and prospective projects together exceed the utility’s all-time peak load of 23,753 MW, set on July 20, 2011. To distinguish firm development commitments from speculative requests, Exelon has introduced transmission security agreements.These agreements require large customers to make financial commitments tied to their requested load, which protects existing ratepayers if projects fail to materialise. Khouzami stated that the pace and scale of anticipated electricity demand have fundamentally changed the company’s approach to grid investment, resource adequacy, and long-term planning.
### Advocating for Regulated Generation

Khouzami argues that PJM’s capacity market has struggled to attract new generation because its short-term price signals provide insufficient revenue certainty for projects. These projects typically take years to develop and build.Exelon estimates that electricity supply costs account for roughly 75 per cent of the increase in its customers’ average electric bills since 2021. The utility is consequently advocating for greater state involvement in resource planning and legislation.This legislation would allow regulated utilities to propose, build, and own generation alongside independent power producers. Exelon is also pursuing utility-owned battery storage, including a proposed 500-MW project in southern New Jersey, to help manage peak demand and wholesale electricity costs.Khouzami believes Exelon will own regulated generation again within five years. He told POWER that the market forces do not incentivise competitive developers to build in PJM, making utility generation a necessary part of the solution.

stories.title: Memphis councilors reject 18-month data center moratorium
stories.summary: Instead, they ban new projects for 135 days
stories.content:
Proposals for a data center moratorium of up to 18 months in Memphis, Tennessee, have been rejected by councilors.

At a meeting on Tuesday, members of Memphis City Council instead voted for a 135-day pause on new data center applications, to coincide with a 90-day review into the impact of digital infrastructure projects in the city, which was commissioned by Paul Young, mayor of Memphis, at the start of October.

The 18-month moratorium plan has been under the microscope for some weeks, and *DCD* reported earlier this month that lawmakers had postponed a vote on the proposal, put forward by councilor JB Smiley Jr., following a controversial meeting attended by more than 100 members of the public, most of whom opposed data centers. This meeting, on October 6, reportedly ended in protests and fights outside the council chamber.

In a vote on the moratorium, which came after a five and a half hour debate, councilors were split 6-6 on whether to enact the data center ban, with one member absent. Instead, they voted for an alternative that will ban data center projects for a much shorter period, pending the outcome of Mayor Young’s review, which it is hoped will “develop clear, actionable recommendations for regulating large and hyperscale data centers in Memphis.”

Hundreds of residents attended this week’s meeting, according to local outlet Action News 5, with 407 able to fit into the council chamber, and dozens of others watching proceedings on screens outside. This number included six people initially banned by the council for violating its speech and decorum policy at the October 6 meeting. However, the ban was lifted by a judge this week, who said the council’s actions were unreasonable.

Memphis does not have a big data center market, but is home to several facilities operated by Elon Musk’s xAI, now rebranded as SpaceXAI, or SpaceXSI.

Developed over the last two years, the data centers, which power the company’s Grok chatbot as well as offering cloud services to clients including generative AI company Anthropic, have been the subject of multiple lawsuits, with environmental and civil rights campaigners claiming xAI has violated its permits when it comes to the use of gas turbines, which have helped the company bring its data center online quickly.

While opposition to the data centers in Memphis is considerable, some councilors said a moratorium would be harmful to economic development in the area, as data center companies could take their tax dollars to other areas. One of Musk’s data centers is already located across the state border in Mississippi.

Data center moratoriums have become commonplace in communities across the US as backlash against AI and data centers grows, with some bans even being introduced at the state level.

stories.title: Russian forces destroy GigaCenter data center in Kyiv, Ukraine
stories.summary: As Ukrainian forces attack telecoms facilities in Russian-occupied Donetsk and Luhansk
stories.content:
Ukrainian data center firm GigaCenter has seen its facility in Kyiv taken out by Russian attacks.

Ukrainian forces, meanwhile, have struck two telecommunications facilities in Russian-occupied territory

## GigaCenter data center in Kyiv hit

It is the latest facility damaged or destroyed in a series of ongoing attacks against digital infrastructure in Russia and Ukraine.

The facility was struck yesterday afternoon (Tuesday, October 20), and appears to be permanently disabled. GigaCenter’s website is currently offline at the time of writing.

“On October 20, as a result of a Russian strike, the GigaCenter data center was critically damaged and disabled,” the company said in a post to social media. “All our employees are targeted. However, unfortunately, we are forced to stop our work indefinitely.”

GigaCenter operates a single data center in Kyiv, built to Tier III standards. The 1,200 sqm facility has a total IT whitespace of 550 sqm (5,920 sq ft) and capacity for around 300 racks. The site opened in 2014. Some online sources list the facility as located at Vasylkivska St, 37B in the southwest of the city.

The company is part of GigaGroup, which was founded in 2006 and includes telco GigaTrans, cybersecurity firm GigaSafe, and cloud operator GigaCloud.

In its own post, GigaCloud said: “Yesterday, a Russian strike damaged one of the data centers hosting GigaCloud’s cloud services. All our clients’ services continue to operate normally on backup decentralized sites in Ukraine and the EU.”

GigaCloud says it operates out of five data centers in the European Union, relying on colocation providers such as Equinix (WA3 in Warsaw, Poland), Atman (Warsaw), and Talex. The company is also an OVH partner. According to its website, the company also has capacity in BeMobile’s data center in Kyiv and another facility in Lviv.

GigaTrans said: “One of the root nodes of the GigaTrans network was damaged. Thanks to geographical redundancy and reliable duplication of network elements, all GigaTrans services continue to work and are provided in full. The main thing is that our employees were not injured and are safe.”

## Ukraine forces target data centers in occupied territories

This week the Ukrainian Armed Forces said its military had hit command and control points of Russian forces in the occupied Luhansk region and near Kurakhove in the Donetsk region.

Local press reports drones struck telecommunications facilities in the Russian-occupied cities of Donetsk and Luhansk operated by Russian-controlled telecoms firms, Ugletelecom and Lugacom.

The Luhansk facility was reportedly operated by Ukrtelecom until Russian forces took over and its operation fell to Lugacom.

ATESH (АТЕШ), which describes itself as a military movement of Ukrainians and Crimean Tatars, this week claimed to have disrupted communications around the IXcellerate data center in Russia, located near Moscow. In a post to Telegram, the group shows a telecommunications box being set on fire. The group said the Russian military uses the facility for communications, including command and control channels and air defense systems.

## Data centers become targets in ongoing conflict

The conflict between Ukraine and Russia has been ongoing since 2014, with significant escalation in 2022 after Russian forces conducted a large-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks on each other's digital infrastructure in recent weeks.

Russia has launched multiple drone strikes against infrastructure in Ukraine, including an attack on Kyivstar’s headquarters.

Facilities around Kyiv operated by Parkovyi Data Center, UTELS, MiroHost, Datagroup, Vodafone Ukraine, De Novo, Cosmonova, Omega Telecom, Ukrsibbank, and Ukrtelecom have been hit in recent weeks.

Outside Kyiv, facilities operated by Tenet in Odesa and the RX-Name data center in the Nikolaev/Mykolaiv area of southern Ukraine have also been hit.

Ukraine has struck back with multiple attacks on Russian-owned digital infrastructure, including strikes on several data centers owned by Yandex and Sberbank. Earlier this year, Ukrainian forces struck a data center in Russian-occupied Ukraine in Prymorsk.

Russian officials have been discussing mitigating measures for attacks on its data centers, ranging from building “doomsday” data centers to siting facilities in disused coal mines or friendly neighboring territories.

Several Starlink ground station sites in Europe, including in Poland, Bulgaria, and Lithuania, have been targets of arson attacks in recent weeks, with officials linking the incidents to Russia. This comes as Elon Musk has been accused of reducing Starlink's available satellite communications capacity in Ukraine.

stories.title: Vantage signs 1GW solid-state transformer supply deal with Heron Power
stories.summary: Will supply the data center firm with its Heron Link SST
stories.content:
Data center firm Vantage has signed a deal with Heron Power, a US solid-state transformer manufacturer, to secure more than 1GW of the company’s SST’s to deploy across its hyperscale data center portfolio.

The deal is expected to support Vantage’s move to deploy 800 VDC racks across its data center portfolio. According to Heron, its Heron Link SST is designed to address the challenges of AI racks, which have much higher densities and more variable loads. It does so by using integrated energy storage, reducing conversion stages and simplifying the path from the grid to the rack.

According to the companies, the agreement will enable faster time to power, greater efficiency, with the Heron Link targeting more than 98.5 percent efficiency from medium voltage to 800VDC, lower infrastructure requirements, and greater energy flexibility.

According to the company, Heron Link is a 5MW modular megawatt power converter built on the latest advances in wide-bandgap semiconductors. In addition, the company claims that the product is designed for high power density and ease of maintenance, offering greater reliability and lower costs for renewable energy storage and data center developers.

“Our customers need a faster and more efficient way to deploy increasingly power-dense and flexible AI infrastructure,” said Curtis Aubry, vice president, global product strategy at Vantage. “By simplifying the electrical architecture and integrating power conversion, energy storage and compute more effectively, we can help reduce deployment complexity, improve efficiency and accelerate our customers’ speed to capacity.”

“Heron was founded to modernize electrical infrastructure and enable an electrified economy,” added Drew Baglino, founder and CEO of Heron Power. “By partnering with Vantage to deploy more than a gigawatt of Heron Links in data centers, we will move 800 VDC from a reference architecture concept to a repeatable, deployed platform, delivering power from grid to rack in an integrated system.”

Heron Power was founded in 2024 by former Tesla senior executive Drew Baglino and is based in Scotts Valley, California. In August, it announced the selection of Morgan Hill, California, as the home of its first large-scale factory, which, when up and running, is expected to manufacture up to 10,000 Heron Links every year, representing 40GW on an annual basis.

The selection of its first manufacturing facility closely followed the close of its Series B funding round earlier this year, which saw the company raise $140 million and brought its total funding to date to $183m. It closed its Series A funding round last May.

The company has already partnered with data center firms to deploy its solution. Last June, the firm signed a Letter of Intent (LOI) with Crusoe to supply power converter technology for the Stargate data center campus in Texas.

stories.title: SC Capital Partners invests in 40MW data center in Pohang, South Korea
stories.summary: Data center being developed with NeoAI Cloud
stories.content:
Singapore's SC Capital Partners Group has invested in a data center project in South Korea.

Set to offer 40MW of gross power capacity, the data center will be located in Pohang and is being developed in partnership with neocloud startup NeoAI Cloud.

SC Capital Partners has not disclosed how much it has invested in the project.

The data center project has also secured investment from government-backed capital.

According to the companies, thus far the data center has received power approval, building permits, and construction has begun on the site. It is currently targeting completion by the end of 2027, and will be designed to support AI workloads, including liquid-cooled infrastructure ready for Nvidia Vera Rubin systems.

The first phase will span 100,000 sqm (1 million sq ft). As of July of this year, around 2 trillion won ($1.35 billion) had been invested in the project.

The site will be NeoAI's first data center, and the company will initially offer colocation services from the site.

Jonathan Yongwan Jo, CEO of NeoAI Cloud, said: “We are pleased to secure this investment from SC Capital Partners, a leading investment firm in Asia Pacific real estate and digital infrastructure. The Pohang AI data center is envisioned to go beyond traditional colocation by leveraging high-density infrastructure space integrated with GPUaaS (GPU-as-a-Service) and AI platform capabilities to provide a high-performance foundation for global enterprises to develop AI models and operate services. Building on the successful delivery of this initial 40MW phase, we plan to advance a second phase expansion of 260MW and look forward to a continued partnership with SC Capital Partners.”

Suchad Chiaranussati, chairman and founder of SC Capital Partners, added: “We are excited to complete this investment, which represents our continued expansion into digital infrastructure in Asia Pacific. The development benefits from strong underlying fundamentals and is well positioned to serve the evolving requirements of the digital economy. We remain focused on identifying high-quality opportunities, particularly in South Korea, where strong policy support for AI and digital infrastructure is contributing to a favorable environment for the sector, and working with experienced local partners to deliver investments that create long-term value for our investors.”

Singaporean real estate investment firm SC Capital Partners has a data center company of its own called Zeus, which it launched in 2023 as a joint venture with Abner Investments. In August of this year, the company signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with SB Telecom Singapore – a subsidiary of SoftBank - and Malaysian IT consultant Robust HPC to build data centers in Southeast Asia.

Pohang is a city on South Korea’s southeastern coast located in Gyeongsang Province. It is not a major data center hub.

stories.title: Envision commissions GW-scale AI data center campus in China
stories.summary: Envision has commissioned its Galaxy Campus, a GW-scale AI data center in Ulanqab, China, as the first flagship project of Mission Gobi. The facility features a 120,000-square-metre supercomputing area designed to support one million AI accelerators.
stories.content:
Envision has commissioned its Galaxy Campus, a GW-scale artificial intelligence (AI) data center in Ulanqab, China, marking the concretisation of Mission Gobi.The campus features a 120,000-square-metre AI supercomputing facility. This facility is designed to deliver one million PFLOPS of computing capacity. It will support up to one million AI accelerators at full build-out. The campus could scale beyond 2 gigawatts (GW).Mission Gobi envisions developing 5 GW of green AI data center capacity in desert and arid regions worldwide by 2030. Envision's Founder and CEO Lei Zhang first presented Mission Gobi at VivaTech in Paris in June 2026.
### Energy-first design

The campus power system integrates renewable generation, dedicated transmission infrastructure, large-scale energy storage, and intelligent controls. This approach aims to maximise output and deliver stable power to AI clusters. Envision treats energy as part of the computing architecture, not as a utility connection.Ulanqab, located in Inner Mongolia, China, provides abundant renewable resources and an annual average temperature of about 4.3°C. This temperature offers natural 'free cooling', reducing energy use and operating costs. The location is approximately 300 kilometers west of Beijing.Envision enters the AI infrastructure sector as a renewable-energy systems company. This enables the design of generation, grid, storage, and compute as one integrated system. Ricky Zheng, Head of Envision's AIDC business, stated that power availability, network performance, and energy efficiency are limiting factors for AI buildout.International peers like US-based Crusoe AI Data Centers and Portugal's Start Campus are also prioritising energy-first solutions. Start Campus is engineered for a 1.2-GW renewable-powered AI campus. If replicated, Mission Gobi would export a systems approach: building compute where renewable energy is plentiful and orchestrating delivery with innovative power systems.

stories.title: Tata Power eyes 2.8GW of generation, transmission, and distribution for Indian data center sector
stories.summary: Current estimates have the Indian data center market reaching 26.3GW by 2031-32
stories.content:
The power arm of the massive Indian multinational conglomerate Tata has announced plans to construct more than 2.8GW of power projects to meet the energy demands of India’s data center boom.

According to the company, the agreement will cover renewable energy, transmission, and distribution projects.

The pipeline comprises about 430MW of upcoming load on its distribution network, 1,236MW of transmission-linked opportunities, and 1,150MW of green energy capacity under active engagement. Tata Power now has 29 active workstreams across 18 data center operators, which it did not disclose.

The company also said it offers powered land, transmission and grid connectivity, renewable energy, storage, cooling, and utility infrastructure to hyperscalers and data center developers.

Within the Mumbai metropolitan region, the company said it will upgrade its 110kV and 220kV network by adding transformation and transmission capacity and building in redundancy. It is also developing new receiving stations and a 400kV transmission ring network. The work is part of its ₹15,000 crore ($1.6 billion) Mumbai Grid Upgradation and Expansion Plan.

Tata Power is one of the largest vertically integrated power companies operating in India. According to its latest numbers, the company has an operational generation capacity of 16.7GW, 7.8GW of which is characterized as clean energy capacity.

Current estimates by the Central Electricity Authority project that AI data centers could add approximately 26.3GW of electricity demand in India by 2031-32. Tata is a key player in this market, with its data center arm, Tata Communications, reportedly operating around 22 data centers in 16 markets across five countries: India, the UK, Singapore, Portugal, and the US.

In July, it was reported that the company acquired land parcels in southern and western India for data centers that could be used by OpenAI.

stories.title: Water harvesting firm Aquaria launches pilot for modular onsite water supply system for data center sector
stories.summary: First units to be shipped in Q3 2027
stories.content:
Austin, Texas-based water-harvesting company Aquaria Technologies has announced a new offering for the data center sector.

The company this week announced that it was opening applications for a pilot of its Hydrogrid product, a modular system that provides data center operators with on-site water supply made directly from the air.

Each unit is shipped in a 40-foot container and, according to the company, can produce up to 5,300 gallons of water every day. The company states that due to its modular nature, it can be stacked, allowing for much larger production levels. In the release, the company states that a 50-unit field deployment could produce up to 265,000 gallons per day across less than four acres.

According to Aquaria, the units sit on a concrete pad and can be commissioned in a matter of weeks. They also can be connected to the site's existing water storage and treatment, with no changes to how the facility is cooled. The company also said that the system can be retrofitted onto existing facilities, with developers able to add units as each phase of the campus is constructed, with prices locked in up front, for both new and existing facilities.

The first units are expected to be shipped in Q3 2027, with pilot partners provided with first access. In addition, selected partners are expected to receive site-specific water production modeling and work with Aquaria.

“Water is now a schedule risk and an approval risk,” said Brian Sheng, co-founder and CEO of Aquaria. “Hydrogrid lets developers bring their own water infrastructure with them, scale it with construction, and take that risk off the table.”

Aside from the pilot projects, the company is also launching a community engagement program for developers, hyperscalers, and public officials to support water neutrality and security within communities that host data centers. The program will support deploying units in homes and public buildings near data center campuses, including schools, fire stations, and community centers.

Aquaria was founded in 2021 and has raised more than $117 million in total funding to support the development of its system. The pilot program is its first publicized project focusing specifically on the data center market.

Water reuse and sustainability are becoming a hot-button topic in the sector, especially within the US market, which has seen more than 15 states weigh bans or moratoriums for new data centers this year, with water use cited as a key factor.

As a result, several major hyperscalers have moved to deploy closed-loop cooling systems. In addition, water reuse and recycling companies, such as Gradiant, have developed data center-specific systems to support more efficient water circularity and use.

stories.title: Amazon withdraws application for data center campus at GWU site in Ashburn, Virginia
stories.summary: Cloud giant backs off proposals after pushback from Loudoun County officials
stories.content:
Amazon has withdrawn plans for a data center campus in Northern Virginia’s Loudoun County, the heartland of the global data center industry.

Amazon has agreed to withdraw its application to develop a data center at the George Washington University Science and Technology Campus in Ashburn, Loudoun County.

In a post on social media, Loudoun Board of Supervisors Chair Phyllis Randall said she and the county attorney and administrator had held meetings with Amazon “over many weeks,” concluding with a new agreement known as “Project Potomac Promise.”

“My goal was to disallow any data centers or infrastructure that could support data centers on this property,” she said. “Through our collaborative conversations, Amazon has agreed to withdraw its proposed application and – of note – forego any legal action to realize data center development on this site.”

Amazon acquired the 122-acre campus from George Washington University (GWU) in March. The site, located along George Washington Blvd, was acquired by Amazon Data Services for $427 million on a five-year sale-leaseback basis, giving the university time to relocate and the cloud company time to secure planning permission.

Amazon had hoped to develop a four-building campus totaling 800,000 sq ft (74,320 sqm) known as the Bridgefield Tech Center. However, strong opposition from local residents, students, and an increasingly anti-data center county board saw major pushback against the proposals.

As part of the newly announced agreement, however, Amazon will dedicate roughly 25 acres of land to Loudoun County, valued at around $65m. Randall said the parcels were “ideal” to develop as a new Community Arts Center and Indoor Sports Facility.

Amazon has further committed to rezone the remainder of the land for mixed use and needed residential uses, including attainable and market-rate housing. The firm has also made a $5m donation to the county’s housing fund.

“I want to thank Amazon for their willingness to meet and engage,” Randall said.

Josh Weissman, VP for data center capacity delivery at Amazon, added: "Amazon has been building in partnership with Loudoun County for 20 years, and we deeply value that relationship. Today, more than 3,400 Amazon employees live in Loudoun County. Our team moved to seize this opportunity when approached by the University about a sale, but as we heard the community's pointed concerns about data center development at this particular site, we took them seriously.”

Earlier this month, Loudoun County staff told the board of supervisors that Amazon would need additional county approval before starting work on any data centers on the property, citing a zoning determination stating that data centers were not permitted as a primary use on the property.

Weissman continued: “While we see the property's legal development potential differently than the county does, we concluded that the best outcome for all is to come together on a shared vision for this campus rather than engage in costly litigation. Project Potomac Promise reflects that choice, and we look forward to working with Chair Randall, the county staff, and development partners to move this plan forward. Given Loudoun's proximity to Amazon's corporate and retail operations, we appreciate the need to expand attainable housing options as the county experiences rapid growth."

Northern Virginia is the world’s major data center hub, with hundreds of facilities totaling gigawatts of capacity in the area. Much of this capacity is centered around Loudoun County, with Amazon owning or leasing a large number of facilities in the area.

Recent years, however, have seen county officials push back on data centers as more and more facilities have been built.

Officials have removed data centers as a by-right zoning option and are exploring removing by-right status from sites that were previously grandfathered in. Both county- and statewide moratoriums on new developments are also being considered.

stories.title: NorthC breaks ground on data center in Geneva, Switzerland
stories.summary: First phase of 4.5MW facility due live in 2028
stories.content:
European data center firm NorthC has started construction on a new facility in Geneva, Switzerland.

“This is a milestone for NorthC and another significant step in our growth in the DACH region,” the company said on LinkedIn this week. “A big thank you to HIAG and our other partners, the local authorities and everyone who made this special moment possible. We look forward to welcoming our first customers here soon.”

Plans for a Geneva data center were first announced in January 2026. Located at Rte du Nant-d'Avril 152 in Meyrin, the modular facility will offer 4.5MW of IT capacity across 5,400 sqm (58,125 sq ft), delivered in increments of 1.5MW. Construction is expected to be completed by Q2 2028.

NorthC said the new facility will use a waterless cooling system, support direct-to-chip liquid cooling, and utilize HVO instead of diesel for its backup generators. It will make its waste heat available for local heating networks.

NorthC managing director for Switzerland, Urs Bürgisser, added: “Proud to have been part of the groundbreaking ceremony for our new Geneva data center in Meyrin last week. An exciting milestone and another step forward for NorthC in supporting Switzerland’s digital future.”

NorthC was formed in 2019 from the merger of Dutch data center firms TDCG and NLDC, originally a subsidiary of Dutch telecoms company KPN. Antin Infrastructure Partners acquired the company in December 2025. The company currently has more than a dozen data centers across the Netherlands, eight in Germany, and four in Switzerland, with more in development in all three markets.

The firm entered Switzerland in 2022 with the acquisition of Netrics. NorthC took over three data centers – two in Münchenstein near Basel and one in Biel – with a total floor space of 13,000 sqm (140,000 sq ft) and more than 7.5MW of capacity. The company then acquired a 1.8MW facility outside Zurich a year later from IT services firm Kyndryl in a sale-leaseback deal.

NorthC announced plans for a new facility in Basel in September 2025. The first phase of the new facility, set to launch in mid-2027, will offer 5.5MW across 2,500 sqm (26,910 sq ft).

The company is also expanding its data center in Biel, adding a further 2MW of capacity. Working with Edico Engineering and Tri-Air, the project will focus on the expansion of the cooling supply and the UPS systems, as well as the review of the emergency power systems.

Built in 2018, Netrics acquired the Biel facility in early 2021. The company was already the anchor tenant at the 3,000 sqm (32,200 sq ft) 4MW data center.

stories.title: Duos secures cloud provider as customer for 20MW of data center capacity
stories.summary: Contract worth $700 million, capacity due live next year
stories.content:
Edge data center firm Duos has secured a cloud provider as a customer.

Nasdaq-listed Duos Technologies Group this week announced the signing of a new ten-year colocation agreement for 20MW of facility load with an unnamed “mature publicly traded cloud services provider” in the US.

The agreement represents more than $400 million of total contract value over the initial term and is expected to be deployed in Q2 2027 within Duos’ “expanding portfolio of Edge AI campuses.”

Duos also said it is in “active negotiations” on approximately 100MW of additional powered, data center-zoned land to expand its Duos Edge AI platform.

The company said it is also currently under contract and in active negotiations to secure approximately 100W of additional powered and data center-zoned land across multiple sites in the United States. Approximately 25MW of that is currently under contract across multiple sites in the US, and the company is in active negotiations on an additional 7MW. All site agreements could be finalized by year-end.

Duos CEO Doug Recker said the deal and expansion represented “another significant step in executing our long-term growth strategy.

He said: “These developments reflect the increasing demand we are seeing from customers seeking scalable, power-dense infrastructure that can be deployed quickly and efficiently. Our modular architecture, contract-first approach, and ability to identify attractive expansion opportunities continue to differentiate Duos in the marketplace. As AI, cloud, content delivery, and enterprise computing requirements grow, we believe we are well positioned to quickly expand our customer base and increase contracted revenue.”

Florida-based Duos, which previously developed rail-focused technology offerings, pivoted into data centers in 2024.

The company has also installed several Edge pods in rural locations across Texas, as well as sites in Illinois and Florida. Its pods total 15 racks and 300kW per container, and Duos Edge says that they can be deployed in as little as 90 days. The firm is also targeting a higher-density container offering 1-2.5MW.

The most recent presentation from the company said it aimed to have some 65 pods and 20MW of capacity deployed by the end of 2026, and 250 pods totaling 60MW of capacity by 2028.

The firm has previously secured an unnamed “investment-grade hyperscaler” as a customer for 10MW of capacity, and neocloud NiStar for 2MW in Columbus, Georgia.

Axe Compute recently acquired an AI infrastructure cluster in Columbus from Duos, alongside the latter’s firm’s GPU-as-a-service entity, as part of Duos' pivot to focus purely on colocation. Duos is separately set to provide Axe with multi-location capacity across the US totaling 55MW.

As a result of the sale, Duos said it was now directing its capital exclusively to developing and operating 10-30MW modular colocation sites across the US.

## Duos adds bricks and mortar to container offering

The Columbus site is described as a "bricks and mortar" facility located at 8 Corporate Ridge Parkway and able to offer up to 20MW.

Previously operated by JMF Solutions as its DLI One facility (and by financial technology firm TSYS before that), Duos acquired the site in June.

Duos said over the summer that it would host more than 2,300 Nvidia B300 GPUs that would be operated by Hydra Host for a third-party client. It's unclear if Hydra Host is still involved after the Axe Compute acquisition.

The TSYS data center was built in 1997, with the company reportedly exiting the site after it merged with Global Payments in 2019.

stories.title: atNorth tops out latest data center in Espoo, Finland
stories.summary: Company adding five-story building to campus
stories.content:
Nordic data center firm atNorth has completed structural work on its latest data center outside Helsinki, Finland.

The company this week announced the topping out of its FIN02 expansion in Espoo, Finland.

“The expansion represents another step in atNorth’s continued investment in Finland, strengthening our presence in the Nordics and supporting the growing demand for reliable, high-performance digital infrastructure,” the company said on LinkedIn.

AtNorth’s FIN02 campus is located in Sinimäentie, Espoo. At full build-out, the site will total 40MW across 20,050 sqm (215,815 sq ft). Plans for the original 15MW facility on the site were first announced in 2023, with the facility launching in October 2025.

Construction firm Skanska was tapped for a €100 million ($112m) expansion at the FIN02 site in May 2026. At the time, the company said the project would see development of a new five-story facility totaling 11,200 sqm (120,555 sq ft). Construction began in April 2026 and is set to complete in Q3 2027.

AtNorth was formed as Advania Data Centers in 2012 from three components: Skyrr, a public sector IT specialist in Iceland; Kerfi, a Swedish outfit with roots in a Nokia spin-off called Datapoint; and Hands from Norway.

The company de-merged from the Advania Group in 2017, rebranded to atNorth, and was sold to Swiss investment manager Partners Group in 2021. Equinix and CPP acquired the company earlier this year.

The company currently operates seven data centers across Sweden, Iceland, and Finland, with additional sites under development in Finland, Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

In Finland, atNorth operates two facilities around the capital, Helsinki, that it acquired from former parent Advania in 2023. The company is also developing FIN04, a 60MW project with potential to reach 430MW, in Kouvola. FIN05 is a 230MW project planned in Salo in southwest Finland.

stories.title: Timesfly reduces data hall fit-out to six months
stories.summary: Timesfly claims it can deliver the mechanical and electrical fit-out of a data hall in six months, assuming the civil shell is complete. This significantly shortens traditional data center construction timelines of three to four years.
stories.content:
Timesfly, a firm specialising in mechanical and electrical works, now delivers data hall fit-outs in six months. This timeframe assumes the civil shell is completed and connected to the grid, the company said. It represents a notable acceleration from the industry's traditional three to four-year construction timelines.The company has delivered 4GW of data centre mechanical and electrical works, including 1.5GW of liquid-cooled halls. Timesfly is currently working on large projects in Malaysia and Thailand simultaneously, adapting designs to local regulations while standardising other business processes.
### Accelerating AI compute capacity

Compute demand has risen sharply due to digital transformation and increasing artificial intelligence (AI) requirements. The bottleneck in data centres lies in long-lead electrical and cooling equipment, contractor coordination, and designs outpaced by new GPU chips, the firm argues. Every month a data hall remains unfinished means expensive GPUs wait and compute revenue is deferred, Timesfly noted.The work enabling a six-month build begins before onsite construction. Timesfly uses a library of standardised drawings for traditional and liquid-cooled AI halls and proven power distribution designs. The firm fully models all elements in Building Information Modelling (BIM) to resolve spatial interferences and design conflicts before construction begins.Timesfly's approach shortens detailed design by over 30 per cent and removes most rework that would surface mid-build. Once a design is confirmed, work typically done sequentially is initiated in parallel. Equipment production is scheduled, external power connections are coordinated, and regulatory filings are lodged before the shell is complete.The company reserves annual production capacity with manufacturers of transformers, Uninterruptible Power Supply (UPS) systems, and liquid-cooling systems. It also maintains alternate suppliers in more than one region. Timesfly reports a 100 per cent first-time energisation rate across its projects.
### Long-term operational responsibility

Chairman Peng, with 24 years in data centre mechanical and electrical engineering, said the industry underestimates post-handover challenges. A liquid-cooled hall, for instance, has more joints and connections than an air-cooled one. A small leak might surface months after commissioning as GPU throttling or corroded pipework.“A data center must serve its owner for fifteen or twenty years,” Peng said. “The work we do in six months determines those twenty years. This is a responsibility we take very seriously.”Timesfly positions itself across the full lifecycle, from consulting and design through project management and construction to operations and maintenance (O&M). Liquid-cooled facilities depend on specific routines like coolant quality testing and scheduled seal replacement. These tasks require skills in fluid chemistry and leak monitoring that traditional data centre staff rarely possess.

stories.title: New PCE metric could recover stranded data center power
stories.summary: A proposed Power Compute Effectiveness (PCE) metric aims to help data centers recover stranded power. It complements Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) by focusing on power allocation for compute in retrofit and design planning.
stories.content:
A new metric, Power Compute Effectiveness (PCE), is gaining interest as AI-driven demand strains data center power availability.PCE is designed to show how much of a facility’s provisioned power is structurally available for compute.It also indicates how much power is tied up in cooling, electrical losses, and other support systems, according to proponents.The proposed metric does not replace Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), the industry-standard metric for operational efficiency.Instead, PCE answers how much capacity is truly available for servers within a fixed power envelope, which is critical for retrofit and expansion projects.Bill Kleyman, executive chair of Data Center Programs at AFCOM, sees value in PCE for evaluating retrofits.It helps operators determine how much provisioned power can support IT equipment, Kleyman said.PCE complements PUE by looking upstream at how a data center’s provisioned power is allocated before servers operate.Airsys Cooling Technologies defines PCE as the share of a data center’s provisioned power allocated to compute, as published in an Open Compute Project paper.If a 100 MW facility allocates 70 MW for compute, its PCE is 0.70; the remaining 30 MW covers cooling, losses, and auxiliary systems.Paul Quigley, Chief Strategic Relations Officer at Airsys and a co-author, explained that PCE asks how much of all provisioned power is for compute.
### Application in Design and Retrofits

PCE becomes valuable when operators seek to add compute without expanding their total power envelope.For example, if a 100 MW facility reduces support requirements from 30 MW to 20 MW through redesign, it can support 80 MW of compute.This raises its PCE from 0.70 to 0.80 without increasing total provisioned power.Quigley noted that infrastructure changes to achieve this gain may require significant capital investment.PCE uncovers whether investment in cooling or electrical architecture can reallocate existing power to compute, he added.This is particularly relevant as utility constraints make securing new capacity difficult in many markets.PCE makes existing power allocation visible, helping designers and operators evaluate infrastructure changes to free up IT power.Initial real-world examples in the Airsys/OCP paper show PCE scores of 0.705 for a 20 MW colocation site.A 100 MW hyperscale campus achieved a PCE of 0.79.Quigley suggested older, air-cooled facilities might have PCEs between 0.50 and 0.65, while well-designed liquid-cooled sites could reach high 0.80s.PCE is most useful in design work, retrofits, and capital planning to identify upgrades that can free up IT load.For instance, a cooling retrofit could reduce a 20 MW cooling allocation to 12 MW, making another 8 MW available for compute.In design, comparing two 50 MW designs, one with conventional chilled water (10 MW cooling) and one with warm-liquid loop (5 MW cooling), shows a 5 MW difference in compute capacity on paper.This results in PCEs of 0.74 versus 0.84, decided before construction, Quigley said.PCE can also help with capacity planning, allowing a 40 MW colocation facility to potentially increase compute capacity from 28 MW to 34 MW through infrastructure changes, avoiding a new utility application.At a portfolio level, PCE could help operators compare sites and prioritise investments to free the most IT load.Kleyman stated that PCE's traction will depend on whether it helps operators make better investment decisions.This requires consistent assumptions about cooling, redundancy, and facility boundaries, he concluded.

stories.title: Crusoe plans Spark Liquid modular data center to support latest Nvidia GPUs
stories.summary: 3.5MW deployments expected to serve Crusoe Cloud in 20-50MW clusters
stories.content:
Neocloud Crusoe has developed a liquid-cooled version of its modular data center offering, Crusoe Spark.

Crusoe Spark Liquid supports up to 3.5MW of compute per system, but can be deployed in multiple units up to 100MW, cofounder Cully Cavness told *DCD*. Production is expected to begin next year, from the company's existing factory in Brighton, Colorado.

"It's a five-fold increase in computing density, going from 500kW IT in the \[existing\] air-cooled Spark version to now 3.5MW IT in the liquid-cooled Spark," Cavness, company president and chief strategy officer, said.

The Spark uses closed-loop cooling, so will not consume any additional water beyond the initial filling phase.

Each Spark consists of three shipping-container-sized modules "snapped together," Cavness said. "You can think of it in that form factor at roughly 60 feet long by 50 feet wide," he said, "that's a significant amount of space for things like compute, storage, networking, and we've designed it in a way that there's some flexibility so that over time, you can mix in next generations of chips and what might happen with storage and compute densities."

Currently, the product is firmly aimed at Nvidia's latest GPUs - supporting Nvidia GB300 NVL72 and Vera Rubin NVL72 racks - with all the Spark Liquids set to be produced in 2027 expected to use Nvidia hardware.

"Spark Liquid is one of the first designs that's compliant with DSX Modular," Cavness said, referring to Nvidia's new reference design for modular data centers. "They're also announcing that Spark is the first and only modular data center platform to achieve what they call Nvidia Exemplar status for cloud reliability.

"They've done a bunch of testing on the way we interconnect different Sparks, and they've said that B300s perform in that deployment to the same level of speed and reliability as they do in a large stick-built traditional data center market."

While the company believes that the performance is comparable, it still expects to take the traditional approach for larger-scale builds. "Ultimately, if you're going to go train a frontier model, we think still the large interconnected campus, like our flagship project in Abilene, probably makes sense if you're going toward gigawatt scale.

"\[For Spark,\] we're mostly looking at you know 10MW plus deployments. I think 20-50MW is probably a sweet spot."

All of the modular liquid deployments for next year are currently set to go to Crusoe Cloud, the company's cloud platform. "As you build data center capacity, being able to deliver on time is really important to our customers. A lot of customers tend to do reservations even ahead of deployments, given the supply-demand situation today," Erwan Menard, SVP of product, told *DCD*.

"I expect that over the years to come, we'll understand better where inference happens and how to bring inference closer to the user," he added.

"Not to mention that certain verticals like physical AI are always looking at improving latency, and so if I can scrap a little bit of latency by inferencing closer to, let's say, a fleet of robots in a facility, Spark is perfect for that. We also have demand for sovereign-type deployments, giving you a commitment of resiliency of compute and storage of any data related to the use of the model. I can give you an exclusive region, Edge zone, and you're the only tenant in there, which can be very helpful in certain countries."

In this current era of compute scarcity in a world of overwhelming demand, speed and trust are key to winning business, Menard said.

"If you go to the factory in Brighton, we build the shell, the container, but we also are able to pre-stage networking, which saves us a ton of time once we show up on site. We're looking with our storage vendors on how they can pre-integrate as well, and so everything is really designed for this predictability of ramping the capacity, and that's only because we're vertically integrated."

The company has also increasingly begun building its own gear, Cavness said. "So we go down to making our own switchgear at a factory in Tulsa, Oklahoma. We'll buy breakers and those kinds of components, but we do all of our own sheet metal work all the way through production of the switchgear board itself, including low voltage and medium voltage."

This helps the company deal with some of the supply chain constraints currently slowing the industry's growth, but it still faces others. "The supply chain is something that I think everybody's managing," Cavness said. "There are long leads across mechanical equipment and electrical equipment. You would have heard of a lot of these, but from chillers, CDUs, and transformers, just to name a few."

The other blocker the industry faces is increasingly strong local opposition. Here, Menard is hopeful that the smaller modular approach can avoid some of the pushback faced by megaprojects.

"If I'm able to build a 20-40MW site with similar per megawatt economics \[as a large data center\], it can be a fantastic project from a community view," he said. "We're bringing good tax money into a given community, and we're able to dial how much energy we are going to consume.

"And if I couple it with, in the near future, software feature capabilities around power management, I'm getting a really powerful AI factory that I can put in many communities with a good understanding of the impact on the grid, alongside positive taxes. And, obviously, no impact on water."

stories.title: President Trump: Data center firms should offer local residents dividends to get communities on-side
stories.summary: President says to 'make deals and get data centers built'
stories.content:
US President Donald Trump has suggested data center developers pay local residents direct dividends in order to overcome opposition to new projects.

In a post to his Truth Social platform, Trump said: “If companies want to make their data centers popular, pay the community, and/or individuals within the community, a 'dividend.'”

Trump continued: “I have watched the process closely, and data centers that were highly unpopular in a certain area have become extremely popular when a financial deal is struck.”

The president concluded that companies should “MAKE DEALS, and get them built!”

Many data center developers and operators have long made proffers to local communities when looking to build new data centers. Sometimes totaling millions of dollars, these proffers can include donations to local charities and institutions, as well as funding infrastructure, environmental, and social projects.

Offering hard cash to local residents, however, is a relatively new concept, spurred by widespread growing opposition to data center developments.

In Pennsylvania, real estate firm NorthPoint Development reportedly recently offered residents in Hazle Township $10,000 each as part of a campaign to secure permission for its Project Hazlenut data center campus that is seemingly set to be leased to Amazon. Some local residents called the offer a bribe.

In Kansas, Digital Realty also recently offered every household in De Soto, where it plans to build a data center, $1,000 in utility and property tax credits for ten years. Digital is planning to develop a 600MW campus across 1,440 acres outside Kansas City.

President Trump’s Truth Social post cited how many data center operators and developers now cover their own costs when it comes to grid infrastructure, ensuring that residential payers are less likely to see their bills go up when utilities look to cover costs.

Trump said he had “mandated” this, although his Rate Payer Protection Pledge is not a regulatory requirement. Several states and utilities have introduced more localized requirements for large-load users and/or data centers to pay for their own generation and transmission upgrades, but a national Ratepayer Protection Act failed to pass the US Senate in October.

President Trump did not mention any future plans around potentially mandating that data center developers pay dividends to local communities.

In a report published in September, Washington D.C.-based think tank the Bitcoin Policy Institute proposed data center operators give local residents a yearly dividend to shore up support for new projects.

“A data center dividend is a payment or credit made every year to every household in a county that hosts a data center,” the report suggests. “The payment or credit would be funded by a fixed share of the property tax revenue the county already collects from that data center while still leaving ample funds to finance schools, police departments, and public works projects. Because that revenue is already being collected under rates already on the books, a dividend would require no new tax and would add no cost for the company that builds the facility.”

The report suggests the dividend could be paid as a check or direct deposit to households, or as a credit county citizens receive against a property tax or a utility bill. The report also suggests local officials could use the money to create endowment funds that invest the cash and pay locals their own dividends.
