stories.title: Malaysia tightens rules amid its data center boom
stories.summary: The biggest news so far and potentially carrying the biggest impact in the data center industry in Malaysia is the proposed bill, Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill to regulate the industry. Singapore has already passed its almost similarly named Digital Infrastructure Act two weeks ago, so this is essentially Malaysia’s version and it’s about time. Thailand’s […]
stories.content:
The biggest news so far and potentially carrying the biggest impact in the data center industry in Malaysia is the proposed bill, Digital Infrastructure (Data Centre) Bill to regulate the industry. Singapore has already passed its almost similarly named Digital Infrastructure Act two weeks ago, so this is essentially Malaysia’s version and it’s about time. Thailand’s similar legislation is still under consideration after it was introduced in Parliament recently.

In Malaysia’s case though, the bill has attracted a lot of attention. The country is after all en route to being the largest data center hub in Asia (ex-China) by 2030. Hence, ahead of expected constraints with such huge upcoming gigawatts, the country is starting to tighten the requirements around its booming data center industry.

Essentially, the government wants to ensure the benefits from the enormous investment and consumption of local resources would go to its citizens. Hence, data center developers in Malaysia would soon face closer scrutiny of capacity reservations and greater responsibility for utility costs through the proposed bill and its subsidiary legislations and guidelines.

The proposed law will be submitted to the Cabinet for its consideration in 2027. As the National Economic Action Council (NEAC) headed by the prime minister has already agreed to it, the drafting and passing of the proposed bill in Parliament (likely by 2027) is practically a certainty. Parliamentarians will just have several debates before passing the bill which no doubt will receive blessings from both sides of the political divide.

The scale of the development pipeline explains the urgency. As of July, the Data Centre Task Force has approved 27 projects with estimated investment of RM225.97 billion. More than half will be hosted in Johor (16), while Selangor gets 10 and Negeri Sembilan one. All are under construction except for one.

#### **Reserved vs demand gap**

In terms of reserved power capacity and actual demand, the gap is huge – as of August, actual demand from 45 operating facilities is about 1.37GW while the combined maximum load is 6GW. The proposed bill will likely attempt to resolve this discrepancy.

During this week’s Parliament session, Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Abdul Ghani proposed that data center developers should bear transmission upgrade costs attributable to their projects. And, operators would also be charged for committed electricity capacity they did not use, thus helping to narrow the gap.

But there is an issue here – developers need extra power to cater for future expansion needs while utilities cannot freely redirect capacity that’s already reserved for them. If the proposal gets passed, reserving power ahead of customer demand will henceforth carry financial consequences.

Separately, Deputy Prime Minister Fadillah Yusof proposed a “user-pays” electricity pricing mechanism and higher Connected Load Charges to discourage excessive reservations, alongside work on guidelines for independent generation with self-generation highly encouraged

Fadillah also disclosed 12.3GW of approved electricity supply capacity as of August, against projected maximum sector demand of 8.39GW by 2030. Neither figure represents today’s operating IT capacity.

When it comes to water, approved demand across Johor, Selangor and Negeri Sembilan is about 445.04 million litres daily over 2025–2030. Data centers will now have to account for their own water demand.

With more investment pouring in and capital raising rising in tandem, Malaysia also wants to ensure a larger share of local participation in terms of local content and workforce. Task force approvals now carry a minimum 30 per cent local content requirement, monitored through six-monthly implementation reports.

Meanwhile, the 27 projects approved are expected to generate 4,053 jobs, including 3,523 highly skilled positions, with Malaysians projected to fill 89.21 per cent of those roles.

In conclusion, data center development in Malaysia now sits at a critical juncture. Moving forward means resolving existing and expected constraints including community pushbacks. Rolling out the red carpet is no longer necessary. The goal has been exceeded and what is now needed is tighter rules to regulate the industry so everyone benefits. The uncertainty accompanying this transition phase is a necessary part of the country’s journey to becoming a matured data center hub.

**\*w.media’s Malaysia cloud and datacenter Convention is happening tomorrow, 22nd October, in Kuala Lumpur.**

stories.title: Clearing AI’s real bottleneck
stories.summary: A data hall fit-out that once took years can now be done in six months. Timesfly argues the decisive work happens before construction starts. Around the world, compute demand has risen sharply, pushed by digital transformation and skyrocketing AI demand. The result is a wave of data center construction of a magnitude never seen […]
stories.content:
### A data hall fit-out that once took years can now be done in six months. Timesfly argues the decisive work happens before construction starts.

Around the world, compute demand has risen sharply, pushed by digital transformation and skyrocketing AI demand. The result is a wave of data center construction of a magnitude never seen before. In spite of massive construction efforts in multiple markets, compute demand continues to outrun the industry’s ability to deliver commissioned digital infrastructure. Chips arrive in months; the buildings that house them have traditionally taken years.

Part of the reason revolves around the capital-intensive, laborious nature of building new data centers. Unlike a factory building, the bottleneck in data centers does not lie in civil construction work, but in long-lead electrical and cooling equipment, the coordination of dozens of contractors across disciplines, and designs outpaced by new GPU chips.

This gap carries a direct cost: every month a data hall sits unfinished is a month of expensive GPUs waiting in crates, and a month of compute revenue deferred. Speed of delivery, in other words, is no longer a construction metric but a business one.

#### **The six-month fit-out**

A new breed of firms now say they can deliver AI capacity fast enough to keep pace with demand. Among them is Timesfly, which delivers the mechanical and electrical fit-out of a data hall as quickly as six months. To be clear, this assumes the civil shell is completed and connected to the grid; the customer also cannot make major design changes once the work begins. Yet this is remarkable given that a construction timeline of between three and four years was considered a reasonable timeframe just a few years ago.

And this is not a one-off process when one looks at Timesfly’s track record with data centers. In recent years, the firm has already delivered 4GW of data center mechanical and electrical works, including 1.5GW of liquid-cooled halls. Indeed, Timesfly is currently working on large projects in Malaysia and Thailand, two disparate geographies, at the same time. Given the different regulatory environments, sustaining this pace comes down to a consistent way of working, with highly standardized processes for design, procurement and project management.

Malaysia and Thailand, for instance, have different electrical codes, fire standards, equipment import rules and handover requirements, which can trip up an engineer not already intimately familiar with them. Timesfly’s response to this challenge is to adapt designs to comply with local regulations while maximizing standardization across other business processes: deploy a generic baseline equipment list for all projects with localized adjustments for country-specific certifications, execute centralized procurement and customs clearance, and adopt reusable templates for construction, acceptance and handover modified to satisfy national requirements. This ensures the six-month fast-track delivery capability can be replicated on demand in different countries.

#### **Compressing the build, not the quality**

The work that makes a six-month build possible starts long before workers go onsite. Timesfly maintains a library of standardized drawings for both traditional and liquid-cooled AI halls, proven power distribution designs, as well as tried-and-tested modules. Everything including pipework, ductwork, busbars, cable trays and cabling, fire-protection facilities, electromechanical equipment and supports & hangers is fully modelled in BIM across all disciplines, so clash checks are completed well before construction and installation to resolve all spatial interferences and design conflicts in advance. Timesfly says its approach shortens detailed design by more than 30 percent and removes most of the rework that would otherwise surface mid-build.

Once the data center design is confirmed, work that typically takes place sequentially is initiated in parallel for speedy completion. Equipment production is scheduled, external power connections are coordinated, and regulatory filings are all lodged before the shell is completed. To help customers hedge against long waits for key data center systems, Timesfly also reserves annual production capacity with the manufacturers of transformers, UPS and liquid-cooling systems. It goes a step further and even maintains alternate suppliers in more than one region.

At the data hall, Timesfly’s team members coordinate various aspects of fit-out works spanning civil, electrical, HVAC, ELV, fire protection and commissioning. For consistency, standard construction templates and power-on procedures are used across projects. This matters most at first energization, as it is when construction defects surface all at once. While most issues are mundane, a data hall that fails its first power-on could result in weeks of delays. Timesfly reports a 100 percent first-time energization rate across its projects to date.

#### **The twenty-year responsibility**

Behind the delivery system at Timesfly is Chairman Peng, who has spent 24 years in data center mechanical and electrical engineering. That experience has shaped a clear view of where data center projects go wrong. The industry, he argues, underestimates what happens after handover. A liquid-cooled hall has far more joints and connections than an air-cooled one, and a small leak that shows no symptoms at commissioning can surface months later as GPU throttling or corroded pipework.

The hard part, in his telling, is not the hardware but the engineering discipline that runs from design through to daily operation. Over the years, that view has settled into something close to a philosophy: “A data center must serve its owner for fifteen or twenty years. The work we do in six months determines those twenty years. This is a responsibility we take very seriously.”

This is also why Timesfly does not stop at construction. The company positions itself across the full lifecycle, from consulting and design through project management and construction to operations and maintenance. The O&M end is more than an add-on. Liquid-cooled facilities depend on routines many operations teams have never run, such as regular coolant quality testing, pipe purging and scheduled seal replacement, along with skills in fluid chemistry and leak monitoring that traditional data center staff rarely have.

For operators, the calculus is straightforward. AI chips will keep arriving on schedule. The advantage goes to those whose halls are ready when they do.

stories.title: The Next Evolution of Data Centres Isn't Technology. It's People
stories.summary: With a $3 trillion investment super cycle under way, labour shortages and weak leadership could slow the global AI data centre buildout.
stories.content:
Wed, 21st Oct 2026 (Yesterday)
A great deal of discussion in the data centre industry is currently focused on speed and scale. The sector is building bigger and faster than ever before, mostly to meet demand for AI infrastructure.

In the midst of a $3 trillion investment "super cycle" that's expected to see global data centre capacity come close to doubling by the end of the decade, it's not altogether surprising that the conversation is hyperfixated on the hyperscale. Gigawatt campuses. AI-driven rack densities. Soaring power demand. The race to bring capacity online is relentless. The magnitude of this infrastructure challenge is only matched by the industry's ambition to achieve something monumental.

However, in the background, a less visible challenge threatens to undermine efforts to execute this generational infrastructure buildout. The real hurdle facing data centre builders in the race to deliver a global AI infrastructure buildout has little to do with silicon chips, liquid cooling, or supply chain worries. In the age of AI, the enduring challenge for the data centre industry is people.

This isn't simply a matter of not having enough people, although staffing shortages are part of the problem. It's a matter of understanding how an organisation gets the best from the people it already has, and how it develops the leaders and culture that enable people to perform.

Meeting this challenge demands a different approach to HR: People Partnering.

People Partnering isn't about doing more HR work, but rather changing the role HR plays in the business.

### People Partnering is more than a traditional HR function

Conventionally, HR is largely viewed as a supporting function. Need an employee issue resolved? Speak to HR. Need a policy? HR. Need advice on compliance? HR. These functions (and the many more HR departments perform) are vital to the smooth running of a business, but they don't capture the full potential value that a People Partnering function can unlock for an organisation.

People Partnering is an effort to move away from the more traditional, transactional, back-office model of HR and towards a system where the department works alongside business leaders to build people and organisational capability and support business objectives.

As data centre projects expand and delivery timelines contract, this is creating new kinds of complexity for data centre builders, which a People Partnering approach to HR can help mitigate. A People Partner should understand the business they support in terms of strategic direction, expected challenges, and its people (including its leaders). They should be close enough to recognise problems when they arise and confident enough to challenge a leader when necessary.

### The difference is being part of the conversation

HR has a reputation for being a reactive function of the business. A People Partner shouldn't be waiting for a problem to arrive in their inbox. Ideally, they've been a part of the conversation all along.

If a business is growing but its leadership capability isn't keeping pace, that's a people issue. If a technically exceptional engineer is promoted into a leadership role without the skills to lead a team, that's a people issue. If a team is struggling with communication, accountability or culture, that's a people issue.

The role of the People Partner is to bring that perspective into the room early enough to make a difference - ideally removing key pain points long before they impact the business' performance. That means advising, coaching, and challenging leaders and their ideas. It means helping them understand the impact of their decisions on the people they oversee and, ultimately, how that will affect the performance of the business.

### Why it matters in data centres

The data centre industry is a prime example of a sector where a more proactive approach to people management is needed.

A data centre project is a profoundly complex operation. From construction and design to commissioning, project teams are increasingly international and multicultural. The data centre boom is putting programmes under significant time pressure. In environments like this, technical expertise is critical, but so too are communication, collaboration and leadership.

The industry is already facing significant pressure on skilled labour. New data from Turner & Townsendshows that demand for AI data centres is exacerbating existing labour shortages, from construction personnel through to specialist engineers, electricians, and commissioning agents.

But the answer isn't just to increase headcounts. Once those people are in the business, what happens next matters just as much. They need to be led effectively by managers equipped to manage increasingly diverse and geographically dispersed teams. Strong people should be developed into capable leaders. And, when things go wrong, organisations need to identify and mitigate problems early enough to prevent them becoming performance, retention or cultural issues.

### The leadership gap

The industry has rightly spent a lot of time discussing the skills gap in terms of engineers and construction workers, but there is another gap forming too at leadership level.

The sector has built up enormous technical expertise over the last decade, but experience doesn't transfer automatically when people move on, or up.

Data centre companies can't afford to simply promote their best technical employees and assume they will become great leaders. Technical expertise and leadership expertise are different capabilities.

People Partners have a role in helping businesses identify and close the gap between those skillsets. They can help determine who has the potential to lead, what experience they need to make the transition, and how to close those gaps.

### Culture isn't an HR initiative

The same applies to company culture.

Culture isn't something the HR team owns. It's created by leaders, reinforced by managers, and experienced by everyone else in the organisation. Culture determines how people perform when a project is under pressure. How challenges are handled and whether or not people feel able to speak up when they see a problem. Culture determines whether accountability is consistent, and ultimately whether people trust the people leading them.

A People Partner can't create that culture for a business, but they can help leaders understand and deliberately shape it into something that benefits the organisation and everyone working within it.

However, doing so requires a People Partner to be close to the business, while remaining independent enough to say what leaders may not always want to hear.

### People are the competitive advantage

Technology can be bought. Equipment can be replaced. Processes can be replicated.

The culture an organisation builds, the leaders it develops, and the trust between its people are far less replicable and replaceable.

In the current data centre landscape, culture has become the principal source of competitive advantage, and the organisations that consistently deliver complex programmes under pressure will not just be the ones that have the best technical expertise or the deepest pockets. They will be the ones that know how to develop culture, support and challenge their people and create the necessary conditions for them to perform at the highest level.

That is what we mean by People Partnering. It isn't HR by a different name; it's a different kind of relationship between the people function and the business.

And as the data centre industry continues to scale, that relationship will become increasingly important, because the infrastructure may be what we build, but people are what make it work.
